motor_endplate_zones.reference_line_from: the proximal end of the arm segment (acromion)
motor_endplate_zones.notes: The clinic's own landmark for the same target is 4-6 cm proximal to the lateral epicondyle, where the radial nerve runs along the humerus and the muscle's maximum thickness lies medial to it. The source states the location as 'the distal third of the arm', which is rendered here as 67-100% of that segment. That is arithmetic on the source's own words, not an inference about the anatomy; no narrower band is claimed than the source gave.
motor_endplate_zones.source: Diaconu S et al. (Elias University Hospital), 'A Visual Guide to Ultrasound-Guided Botulinum Toxin Injection in Spasticity: Part II -- Proximal Upper Limb Muscles', Toxins 17(6):276 (2025), doi:10.3390/toxins17060276 -- review synthesis of the intramuscular neural arborization literature it cites (Yi, Li, Yang, Moon and others)

ultrasound_injection_approach.transducer_placement: Transverse on the anterolateral arm at the distal third, about 4-6 cm proximal to the lateral epicondyle.
ultrasound_injection_approach.depth_layer: Superficial to the humeral cortex; biceps brachii lies medial to it at this level.
ultrasound_injection_approach.identification_cues: The radial nerve is the landmark: it runs along the humerus here, and the muscle's zone of maximum thickness is seen medial to it. Biceps brachii, medial to brachialis, can be confirmed dynamically by asking for forearm supination.
ultrasound_injection_approach.notes: Part I's strategy is the context: brachialis is injected as the only pure elbow flexor, sparing biceps brachii and brachioradialis so that supination is preserved.
ultrasound_injection_approach.source: Diaconu S et al. (Elias University Hospital), 'A Visual Guide to Ultrasound-Guided Botulinum Toxin Injection in Spasticity: Part II -- Proximal Upper Limb Muscles', Toxins 17(6):276 (2025), doi:10.3390/toxins17060276 -- review synthesis of the intramuscular neural arborization literature it cites (Yi, Li, Yang, Moon and others)

trigger_points.location_description: Most often the distal half of the muscle, palpated on either side of the biceps with the elbow flexed and the biceps displaced medially; also a lateral trigger point close to the radial nerve
trigger_points.referred_pain_pattern: Dominant target is the base of the thumb (carpometacarpal region and dorsal thumb web); distal trigger points also refer to the antecubital fossa
trigger_points.activation_perpetuating_factors: Associated trigger points in biceps, brachioradialis, supinator, triceps, and compensatory hand-extensor trigger points when thumb pain leads to compensatory gripping
trigger_points.notes: A taut lateral band where the radial nerve passes between brachialis and brachioradialis can compress the nerve's sensory fibres, producing tingling/numbness on the dorsum of the thumb and first web; thumb-base referral is misdiagnosed as first CMC arthritis or de Quervain tenosynovitis; antecubital tenderness read as 'biceps tendinitis'

clinical.compiled_by: repository owner (physician); elbow_muscles_reference_v2.html, compiled 04/09/2026 (v2; v1 31/08/2026). Strength data come from the Mayo elbow series (An et al. 1981; Askew et al. 1987), from MRI/cadaver architecture studies (Murray et al. 2000; Kawakami et al. 1994) and from Neumann (2017). Values are population means; individual variation is large.
clinical.function_biomechanics: Brachialis is the "workhorse" flexor: a single-joint muscle inserting on the ulna, so forearm rotation does not change its leverage and it is active in slow, fast, loaded and unloaded flexion alike. It has the largest physiological cross-sectional area of the flexors and contributes roughly half of flexion torque despite a moment arm shorter than that of biceps. Peak isometric flexion torque of the elbow occurs near 90° of flexion, where flexor moment arms are longest. The superficial head has the mechanical advantage (more proximal origin, more distal insertion); the deep head, lying parallel to the ulnar collateral ligament, has been proposed as a dynamic anterior sling protecting the ligament, complementing anconeus posteriorly. Capsular fibres, when present, retract the anterior capsule during flexion.
clinical.adjacent_structures: Adjacent bursae: None named; the anterior capsule and the fat pad of the coronoid fossa lie deep to its distal fibres. Adjacent structures and relations: Median nerve and brachial artery lie on its medial anterior surface; biceps and the lateral antebrachial cutaneous nerve anteriorly; radial nerve laterally between brachialis and brachioradialis; the anterior capsule and coronoid deep.

trigger_points.location: Most often the distal half of the muscle, palpated on either side of the biceps with the elbow flexed and the biceps displaced; also a lateral TrP close to the radial nerve, and a proximal TrP.
trigger_points.referred_pain: the dominant target is the base of the thumb (carpometacarpal region and dorsal thumb web); the proximal TrP refers to the anterior deltoid region; distal TrPs also refer to the antecubital fossa.
trigger_points.notes: Symptoms / mimics: Thumb-base pain misdiagnosed as first CMC arthritis or de Quervain tenosynovitis; anterior shoulder ache; restricted terminal elbow extension; tenderness in the antecubital fossa read as "biceps tendinitis". Entrapment: Travell & Simons describe compression of the radial nerve (sensory fibres) by a taut lateral band where the nerve passes between brachialis and brachioradialis, producing tingling and numbness on the dorsum of the thumb and first web. Associated TrPs: Biceps, brachioradialis, supinator, triceps; TrPs in the hand extensors when the thumb pain leads to compensatory gripping.
trigger_points.source: Travell & Simons, vol. 1, 2nd ed., 1999: ch. 31, Brachialis.

pain_referred_into_this_muscle_from: scalenes and subclavius (anterior arm skipping the elbow)
clinical.pain_referred_into_territory: Pain referred INTO this territory from elsewhere
clinical.notes: Heterotopic ossification after elbow trauma or dislocation forms preferentially in brachialis (anterior). The muscle's superficial-head tendon has been proposed as a local graft for annular ligament reconstruction. The brachialis–brachioradialis interval is the lateral gateway to the radial nerve in the distal arm.
clinical.caveat: Clinical reference for professional use; anatomical variation is frequent and trigger-point patterns describe typical, not universal, presentations. Referred pain is presented in both directions: pain that each muscle's TrPs refer to other regions, and pain that other muscles (shoulder, chest, back) and non-muscular sources refer into the elbow region. Where Travell & Simons did not map a muscle separately (extensor digiti minimi, pronator quadratus) this is stated rather than filled in.
